notes_for_us: The brief says keep a contradicted preset option in the handoff, and the emit rules say a set-aside option must not price the route. Those combine to a kept option with no modifier, which is what I did, but nothing in either document says so out loud and a reader of the handoff alone would see building-interior in image_prompt with a P0 route and reasonably call it a bug.

'20 studs next to you' is a relative spawn rule, and count is documented as 'the number the prompt stated for this pick' with examples that are all absolute (five islands, three floors). A first-person viewmodel gun has no destination in this system at all. It is the most visible thing in the user's mental image of their game and it is neither layout nor image as the pipeline means them, so it lands in mechanics, which is where scoring and UI go.

notes_for_us: Every option here traces to the prompt and preset_derived came back empty, which is the first prompt in my batch where the preset added literally nothing. segments with kind 'zone' still demand a shape, and for terrain biomes of one contiguous surface there is nothing to put there. The field rule offers null only for 'a space the user named but never described', which is not this case — these are described in detail, they just are not shaped spaces. The theme table lists 'Stylized / Toon' as a theme, and forty lines later the skill says theme is a setting and never a rendering style and that putting a rendering style there is 'the commonest misfiling there is'. 'Cliffs around map edges' is doing containment work, not landform work. terrain-relief holds the cliffs and loses the fact that they are the boundary. Survival has BoundaryZone as a shape type; there is no boundary option.

notes_for_us: This prompt breaks the P6 gap rule and the skill has no way to record it. Obby's P6 hangs on 11-stud horizontal and 7.2-stud vertical limits at default WalkSpeed, and the prompt's central mechanic is that WalkSpeed increases with height. Infinite Runner has exactly the right rule (spacing = CurrentSpeed x 0.5s) and Obby has no pointer to it, so an obby with variable speed either silently validates against the wrong numbers or has to import a rule from a genre it is not.

'Die and restart' is a positive statement that a near-universal Core option must not be built, and there is nowhere to put that. preset_rejected only exists for options the preset carried; checkpoint-respawn is not in Precision Platformer, so the prompt's explicit refusal of checkpoints is recorded nowhere except a note.

The theme is inferred from one noun ('pyramid') and the skill sanctions that, but Egyptian versus Aztec versus stylised are three different builds off the same word. Naming a structure is a weaker theme signal than naming a place or a game, and the rule treats them the same.

open_questions.ask: Which cue should carry the production tier as the primary read — hex height, glow brightness, or particle density? All three at once tends to make the board noisy; I would pick one and use the others as support.
Do roads, settlements and cities sit on hex edges and corners like Catan, or in the middle of tiles? Corners mean generating a vertex lattice as well as the hexes.
Roughly how many hexes across should the board be, and how many resource types? You mentioned 3-4 tiers per type.
Should it look like a physical tabletop — a rim, a table under it, wooden pieces — or a floating island of hexes in open space?

captured: hexagonal grid as the whole play area
fixed per-hex production tiers replacing dice
tier legibility through height, glow and particle density
3-4 tiers per resource with rare tiers rarer on the board
roads, settlements and cities built adjacent to hexes
adjacency rule: a settlement collects from all touching hexes
real-time continuous economy with no turns
robber as a purchasable targeted steal
data-driven grid generation rather than a hardcoded map

notes_for_us: The load-bearing requirement here is that a per-tile numeric property must be readable off geometry — height, glow and particle density all scaling with output rate. Nothing in the system encodes a property of a tile, only the tile. tile-grid gives an evenly divided board and drops the fact that every cell carries a value the player must be able to see, which is the prompt's whole first rule change.

board-grid is described as Strategy's smallest layout job — 'a table, a board, and seating' — and this prompt is a board with variable tile heights, a vertex lattice for settlements, an edge lattice for roads, and four legibility tiers. The shape is right and its framing badly undersells what it has to carry.

SET was easy to reach and correct, and the stage B two-question split is what got me there rather than the keyword. Worth recording as a rule that worked: 'board game' would have tempted P5 and the second question stopped it.

buildzone-grid and buildzone-plot are both written for a battlefield — one flanks a track, the other radiates from a base. Catan-style legal positions are a fixed discrete lattice, which is neither, so I bent buildzone-plot and the adjacency semantics survive only in the text.

unmatched_options.text: hex size/height, glow intensity, or particle density scales with output rate so a player knows at a glance which hex produces more
settlements and cities at hex corners, roads on hex edges, following Catan's adjacency rule
the Robber, bought then moved onto an opponent's adjacent hex
numerous hex tiles arranged in a compact contiguous layout
persistent per-player resource ledger updated on a server loop

skill_gap.name: no per-tile property encoding
skill_gap.why: the prompt's central requirement is that each hex's production tier be legible from its geometry — taller and brighter means more — and no option can attach a value to a cell of a grid. tile-grid builds the evenly divided board and there is nowhere to say that the cells differ and how the difference must show
